column2: The contested land north of the Ohio River, a no-man's-land since the Beaver Wars that the Iroquois claimed by conquest but did not settle.

column1: Ch6: Albany Congress (Albany Plan of Union)
column2: The wartime meeting where Benjamin Franklin's plan for a federal council of representatives from each colony to run common defense.
The British idea that each member of Parliament stands for the whole empire, so colonists were represented without voting.
The colonial idea that people are represented only by officials they elect who answer to them.
A British order that stopped colonial settlement west of the Appalachians and made the western lands Indian territory.
A direct tax for revenue on legal documents, customs papers, newspapers, almanacs, diplomas, playing cards and dice.
A law stating that Parliament could make laws for the colonies "in all cases whatsoever," leaving unclear whether that included taxes.
Duties on imported lead, paint, paper, glass and tea whose revenue paid royal governors, judges and customs officers.
An intercolonial network of committees that shared statements of rights and grievances and spread resistance into rural areas.
A law giving the bankrupt East India Company a monopoly on selling tea directly to America, making tea cheaper but still taxed.
Four laws punishing Massachusetts: closing Boston's port, ending its self-government, letting officials be tried elsewhere, and quartering troops in private buildings.
A law giving former French Canada a government with no elected assembly, recognizing the Catholic Church, and extending it to the land between the Mississippi and Ohio Rivers.
Thomas Paine's pamphlet attacking monarchy and arguing the colonies were destined for independence.
William Pitt took over the war, had Britain pay for it and respect colonial militias, and won Indian allies, turning defeat into victory.
Pontiac was the Ottawa chief who embraced Neolin's message and led the 1763 attacks that captured British forts west of Detroit.
Patrick Henry was a young Virginia Burgess who introduced the Virginia Resolves denying Parliament's right to tax.
The Sons of Liberty were traders, lawyers and prosperous artisans who organized seaport crowds to intimidate stamp distributors and customs collectors.
Samuel Adams was a Massachusetts master organizer who sent the circular letter, started the committees of correspondence, and helped lead resistance in Boston.
John Adams was a defense lawyer for the soldiers tried after the Boston Massacre.
The regular, long-term army that the Second Continental Congress created, led by Washington.
Local part-time citizen-soldiers who turned out only when the British came near.
Americans who backed the king and Parliament.
German mercenary soldiers hired by Britain.
An open revolt by soldiers against their officers.
Guerrilla-style fighting between rebel and loyalist bands.
A petition affirming loyalty to George III and asking him to disavow his ministers.
Lord Dunmore's offer of freedom to slaves who joined the British.
The statement that all men are created equal with unalienable rights, that government rests on consent, and that George III's abuses justified breaking away.
An elected body that replaced a royal colonial legislature and took over government.
The Continental Army's winter camp near Philadelphia, marked by hunger, cold and disease.
Thomas Jefferson did most of the drafting of the Declaration of Independence.
Lord Dunmore was Virginia's royal governor who offered freedom to slaves who joined the British and shelled Norfolk.
Joseph Brant was the bilingual, literate Mohawk leader of the Iroquois warriors who aided the British.
Daniel Morgan led part of Greene's army and routed Tarleton at Cowpens.
The English-born writer of Common Sense, which attacked monarchy and urged independence in 1776.
The 1777 American victory where Burgoyne surrendered, convincing France to ally with the United States.
The 1781 French and American victory where Cornwallis surrendered, ending Britain's will to fight.
The organization of a United States, dividing power between the national and state governments.
The first national framework, which left the power of the purse and final lawmaking to the states.
Opponents of the Constitution who pushed for a bill of rights.
A way of life in which farm families lived mainly on what their own land and labor produced, bartering any surplus locally.
A way of life in which people sold goods or services in a wider market and lived on their earnings.
The president's advisers who head the executive departments, a system not mentioned in the Constitution.
Hamilton's plan to pay the whole federal debt in full.
Hamilton's plan for the federal government to take over the states' debts.

column1: Ch9: Bank of the United States
column2: A national bank chartered for 20 years in 1791 to hold government deposits and issue banknotes.
A tax on goods made at home, such as Hamilton's tax on whiskey.
Reading the Constitution narrowly so the federal government has only the powers expressly given to it.
The idea that the necessary and proper clause lets Congress use powers beyond those listed, such as chartering a bank.
The 1794 uprising of western farmers against the whiskey excise tax.
The right of nations not at war to trade with warring nations in nonmilitary goods.
Britain's practice of forcing sailors, including Americans, into its navy.
The 1795 treaty with Britain that removed British troops from the Northwest but won no other concessions.
The party led by Hamilton favoring commerce, a strong government, order and ties to Britain.
The party led by Madison and Jefferson favoring agriculture, limited government, strict construction and France.
Washington's 1796 statement warning against the dangers of political parties.
The French demand for a bribe from American envoys that sparked naval war with France.
The 1798 Federalist laws targeting immigrants and punishing criticism of the government.
Madison's and Jefferson's claims that states could interpose against unconstitutional federal laws.
A state's claimed right to place its authority between its citizens and an unconstitutional federal law.
The 1804 amendment requiring electors to vote separately for president and vice president.
Adams's last-minute Federalist judges appointed under the Judiciary Act of 1801.
The power of courts to decide whether laws violate the Constitution.
The 1803 Supreme Court case in which John Marshall established judicial review.
An ideal Ch. 9 names as encouraging girls' academies; the book defines it in Ch. 8, which still needs to be pulled.
Jefferson's vision of the West as enough land for generations of independent farmers.
The 1795 treaty in which tribes ceded most of the land between Lake Erie and the Ohio River.
The 1803 purchase of Louisiana from France for about $15 million, doubling the nation's size.
The Lewis and Clark expedition up the Missouri River to the Pacific.
A multi-day outdoor revival where frontier crowds camped to hear preaching.
The wave of religious revivals that swept the nation after 1800.
Tecumseh's effort to unite many tribes to protect Indian land.
Jefferson's policy of protecting neutral rights through economic pressure instead of war.
The 1807 law banning American ships from foreign ports and all American exports.
Young nationalist Republicans led by Henry Clay who pushed for war with Britain.
The 1814 meeting of New England Federalists opposing the war and proposing amendments.
The treaty ending the War of 1812 that left impressment and neutral rights unresolved.
The 1820 deal admitting Missouri as a slave state and Maine as free and banning slavery north of 36°30′.
The 1819 treaty in which Spain ceded Florida and set a boundary to the Pacific.
Monroe's 1823 warning that the Americas were closed to new European colonization.
